heard: Your elevator comes the wrong way nine times in 10. By the end of this, you'll know exactly why. Why a second elevator barely helps and why the same trick makes your bus late. Here's the building. A lobby and 10 floors above it. You work on floor one, one floor up. You wanna go up, so you press the button. The doors open and the arrow points down. Again, keep a tally for a month and it's the wrong way nine times out of 10. It feels like the building is against you. It isn't. Count every car that passes your floor all day and exactly as many go up as go down. So both directions pass you equally often. And yet the first car you meet is almost always going down. Both are true at once. Start with one elevator that never rests. It rides from the lobby to the top and back down over and over at a steady speed. Draw it tight over time. Up to floor 10, down to the lobby, up again. A zigzag. Now draw a line at your floor. Floor one sits right at the bottom of the zigzag. Look at how much of the zigzag is above your line. Of every 10 floors the car covers, nine are above you. So, dine tenths of the time the car is above you. You walk up and press the button at a random moment. The car doesn't know you're coming. So nine times in 10, at that moment, it's somewhere above you. And a car above you can only reach you on its way down. That's the whole trick. It's not about where the car goes. It's about where it is when you show up. Notice what we never needed. A program, a schedule, or any idea where the car is headed. Just a car that spends nine tenths of its time above you. Now look at the timing. The car passes you going up, climbs nine floors, comes back down nine floors, and passes you going down. That's a long gap, 18 floors of travel. Then it drops one floor to the lobby and comes back one floor, passes you going up again. That's a short gap, just two floors. So the passes alternate. Up, down, up, down. Equal numbers. But every gap that ends with a down car is nine times as long as a gap that ends with an up car. Arrive at a random moment, and you're far more likely to land inside a long gap. 18 out of every 20 moments. Nine in 10. Wrong way. Here's a way to feel it. Stand on floor one with a stopwatch. After an up car passes, a down takes 18 floors of travel to show up. After a down car, the next up car is back in just two. This works on any floor. Your chance of a down car is the share of the building above you. Floor five of 10, a fair coin. Floor eight up eight times in 10. The middle floor is the only one that feels fair. Every other floor gets a building that seems to lean. That's the first answer. If you like seeing the gears behind everyday annoyances, subscribe. There's a new one twice a day. This was first noticed by two physicists, George Gammo and Marvin Stern, who had offices in the same seven -story building. Gammo worked on the second floor. He noticed the first elevator to stop at his floor was usually going down, about five times in six. Stern worked on the sixth floor, one below the top. For him, the first elevator was usually going up, also about five times in six. Put the two complaints side by side, and the answer is right there. Neither elevator was biased. Each man sat in a lopsided spot. That's why it's a paradox and not a fault. Nothing in the machinery favors either direction. The whole bias lives in where you stand. Gammo's floor had one floor below it and five above. Stern's had the opposite. Same zigzag flipped. In 1958, they put the puzzle in their book Puzzle Math, and they added one more line. With more elevators, the situation will, of course, remain the same. It doesn't. In 1969, Donald Knuth wrote a paper on the problem. With two elevators, Gammo's chance of a down car drops from 15 and 18 to 13 and 18. So let's add elevators to your building. A second car running on its own schedule. Now which one reaches you first? With two cars, the wrong way drops from 90 % to 82%. Three cars, 76%. Even with 10 cars, it's still 55%. It creeps toward a coin flip, but slowly. There's a neat pattern hiding in those numbers. One car leans 40 points past a coin flip. Two cars, 32, 3, 25 .6. Each new car keeps eight -tenths of the lean. Why does it shrink at all? Look at the very next moment after you press. Not the whole cycle, just the next second. A car above you is the most likely case, but it's usually far away. Its arrival is spread over 18 floors of travel. A car below you is rare, but it's always close. Its arrival is squeezed into just two floors of travel. Multiply it out. Nine -tenths spread over 18 floors or one -tenths squeezed into two floors. Both give the same chance. One in 20 per floor of travel. So in the first instant after you press, up and down are exactly equal. With one car, you usually wait long enough for the far cars to win. With many cars, someone arrives almost at once and that first instant is a fair coin. That's what Gamo and Stern missed. One car rewards the big side of the building. Many cars only care what happens right next to you. In practice, the lean fades slowly. With six cars in the bank, floor one still meets a down car 63 % of the time. Eight cars, still 58%. So if your building has one old slow elevator, you'll feel this every day. If it has a bank of eight, you'll still feel it, just less. This isn't really about elevators. It happens anytime you show up at a random moment and the gaps are uneven. Your bus. The timetable says one every 10 minutes. But the bus is bunched up, a two -minute gap, then an 18 -minute gap over and over. The average gap is still 10. But nine -tenths of the time, you're standing inside an 18 -minute gap. Your average weight isn't five minutes. It's 8 .2. The fix is spacing, not more buses. Make the same buses come evenly. One every 10 minutes and the average weight falls to five. And the elevator, from floor one with gaps of 18 and two, your average weight is 8 .2 floors of travel. The same numbers, the same trap. Trains do it too. Near the end of a line, the next train is usually heading to the end. For exactly the reason your elevator is it's heading down. Trains, buses, elevators, anything that comes and goes. When the gaps are uneven, a random arrival mostly lands in the long ones. It even fools schools. A school with two classes, one of 10 and one of 50. The school says the average class is 30. Ask the students, 50 of the 60s sit in the big one. The average student is in a class of 43. Same trick. You sample the big things more often because they're big. So the students say classes are crowded and the school says they aren't. Both are telling the truth. Real elevators aren't this tidy. They stop, they wait, they get full. Does the paradox survive? Idle cars often go back to the lobby. Rush hour sends everyone down at once. People on low floors take the stairs. Full cars skip your floor. All of that shifts the numbers, but it doesn't remove the effect. And if you work near the top, you'll feel it even more. Cars are rarely above you. Run it for your own floor. On floor three of a 30 floor tower, 27 of the 30 floors are above you. One car comes down first nine times in 10, same as our building. Two explanations you'll hear are wrong. One, the elevator is programmed to favor the lobby. Our zigzag car has no program at all, and it still does it. Two, you only remember the bad days. But the tally is real. Simulate 200 ,000 button presses on floor one, and 90 % of them meet a down car. So when the arrow points the wrong way, nothing is rigged. You're just near the end of the line. One car, a lopsided spot, and a random moment. That's all it takes for a fair machine to feel unfair. So to sum up, up and down pass you equally often. A single car spends most of its time on the big side of the building. You arrive at a random moment, so you usually catch it there. More cars help but slowly. Your friend works on floor nine of your building, one below the top. There are two elevators, which way does the first car usually come, and how often? Answer in the comments.
